# The language: values, YAML, templates, states

<!-- Generated by tools/handbook. Edit the code, not this file. -->

<!-- kind: reference -->

The first half of halite is a compiler. Text goes in (YAML and Jinja,
written by people), and an ordered list of things to do comes out. These
packages are that compiler, and they know nothing about the network. They are
the oldest code in the tree and the best tested, because the whole premise of the
project is that real trees must compile unchanged.

The path a state file takes: `yaml` and `template` (via `render`, in
`rendersandbox`) turn text into `value` data; `state` compiles that into a low
state; `runner` executes it by calling the functions registered in `states` and
`exec`, whose implementations live in `builtin`, each described by a
`signature`. `target` decides which nodes a top file entry applies to; `pillar`
and `grains` supply the data.

Each entry below is the package's own documentation comment, unedited, followed by
the files it is made of and what it exports. The comments in this codebase are long on
purpose: they say why, and why the obvious alternative is wrong.

## `internal/value`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/value`.

Package value is halite's data model: the nine types the YAML parser is allowed to construct, an ordered mapping, and the source positions that make a diagnostic point at the line an operator wrote.

Ordering is the reason this package exists rather than a plain Go map. State ordering follows declaration order in the SLS file (SPEC section 11.4), so a mapping that loses its order loses the run order with it. A Go map is never used to hold parsed data.

Positions are carried on mapping entries rather than on every scalar. That is a deliberate limit: every diagnostic the specification calls for anchors on a mapping key — a state ID, a module.function, an argument name, a pillar key — or is a parse error, which carries its own position. Sequence items in an SLS tree are themselves single-key mappings and so carry positions of their own.

**Files:** `duration.go`, `json.go`, `merge.go`, `value.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `CanonKey` (func): CanonKey renders a scalar key in the form used for lookup.
- `DecodeJSON` (func): DecodeJSON parses JSON into the ordered model, keeping object key order rather than losing it to a Go map.
- `Deep` (func): Deep returns a deep copy of a value, so that a caller may mutate the result without affecting the original.
- `EncodeJSON` (func): EncodeJSON renders a value as JSON, preserving mapping order.
- `EncodeJSONSpaced` (func): EncodeJSONSpaced renders JSON with Python's separators when spaced is set: `, ` between items and `: ` after a key.
- `Entry` (type): Entry is one key/value pair in a Map, with the positions of both.
- `FromJSON` (func): FromJSON lifts a value decoded by `encoding/json` into the nine-type model.
- `KeyString` (func): KeyString renders a key the way a template or a log line should show it.
- `Kind` (type): Kind names one of the nine types the parser may construct.
- `KindOf` (func): KindOf classifies a value.
- `Map` (type): Map is an ordered mapping.
- `MapOf` (func): MapOf builds a map from alternating key and value arguments.
- `Merge` (func): Merge combines src into dst and returns the result.
- `MergeOpts` (type): MergeOpts controls a merge.
- `NewMap` (func): NewMap returns an empty map with capacity hint n.
- `ParseDuration` (func): ParseDuration reads a duration the way a tree writes one.
- `ParseStrategy` (func): ParseStrategy resolves a configured strategy name.
- `Pos` (type): Pos is a source location.
- `Strategy` (type): Strategy names a merge behaviour.
- `Traverse` (func): Traverse resolves a delimited path such as "a:b:c" against nested mappings and sequences, returning the value and whether the whole path resolved.
- `Truthy` (func): Truthy implements the truthiness rule shared by the template engine and the state compiler: Python semantics, so an empty string, an empty collection, zero, and null are false.
- `TypeName` (func): TypeName gives a human name for any value, including ones outside the model, for use in error messages.

## `internal/yaml`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/yaml`.

Package yaml is halite's YAML parser: the subset of YAML 1.1 that real Salt state and pillar trees contain, and nothing beyond it.

There is no YAML parser in the Go standard library and importing one would breach the dependency policy in SPEC section 4.2, so this is written. The subset is defined by SPEC section 10.1 and is intentionally strict: the parser can construct nine types and has no code path that constructs anything else, which is what stops a YAML document from becoming code execution.

Mappings preserve declaration order, because state run order follows declaration order in the file.

**Files:** `block.go`, `collection.go`, `encode.go`, `errors.go`, `flow.go`, `parse.go`, `scalar.go`, `scalars.go`; with tests.

- `DefaultOptions` (func): DefaultOptions returns the parse options SPEC section 10.1 specifies.
- `Encode` (func): Encode renders a value as YAML.
- `EncodeOptions` (type): EncodeOptions controls rendering.
- `EncodeScalar` (func): EncodeScalar renders a single scalar, quoting it when a plain rendering would resolve to a different type, in the dumper's own style.
- `Error` (type): Error is a parse failure with a source position.
- `IsBool11` (func): IsBool11 reports whether a scalar is one of the YAML 1.1-only boolean spellings.
- `Options` (type): Options controls a parse.
- `Parse` (func): Parse reads a single YAML document.
- `ParseFile` (func): ParseFile reads and parses a file, filling in the file name for diagnostics.
- `ParseStream` (func): ParseStream reads every document in a stream.
- `Quote` (func): Quote renders a string as a double-quoted YAML scalar with the escapes the parser accepts.
- `Related` (type): Related is a second position that explains an error, such as the first occurrence of a duplicate key.

- `WarnKind` (type): WarnKind classifies a lint warning the parser emits while still producing a value.
- `Warning` (type): Warning is a diagnostic that does not stop parsing.

## `internal/template`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/template`.

Package template is halite's Jinja2-compatible template engine.

Existing SLS trees are full of Jinja, and requiring a rewrite to Go's text/template would defeat the point of the project, so the engine is written rather than imported. It is a subset, defined by SPEC section 10.2, and the subset is large enough that a well-formed Salt tree renders unchanged.

Two deliberate departures from Jinja are worth knowing before reading further. Undefined names are strict by default (section 10.2.6), so a missing pillar value is an error naming the file, line, and identifier rather than an empty string that produces a state which silently does the wrong thing. And the random filters are seeded deterministically per render (section 10.2.4), so a test=True run and the real run that follows it agree.

## `internal/render`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/render`.

Package render runs an SLS file through its renderer pipeline: a template stage followed by a serializer stage, named by a shebang-style first line and defaulting to \`#!jinja|yaml\`.

The reason this is a package rather than two calls at each call site is the source map. A YAML error in a heavily templated SLS file must report the position in the .sls file the operator wrote, not the position in the rendered output. Salt reports the rendered position or nothing at all, and diagnosing a templated highstate failure is consequently a well-known misery. Fixing it is a stated goal of SPEC section 10.1.4.

**Files:** `engine.go`, `gpg.go`, `render.go`; with tests.

- `CheckPipeline` (func): CheckPipeline refuses a pipeline this build cannot run.

- `Engine` (type): Engine renders one file.
- `Error` (type): Error is a serializer failure reported at the template position rather than the rendered one.
- `Explain` (func): Explain is what `lint` prints after a file's result line, for the operator who has to work out what went wrong: the whole rendered output when all is set (`--rendered`), and the template source around a template error, which has no rendered output to show.
- `GPGOptions` (type): GPGOptions configure the decryption.
- `InProcess` (type): InProcess renders in the calling process, which is what halite did everywhere before the sandbox existed and still does wherever the sandbox is not turned on.
- `NumberedText` (func): NumberedText is the whole of a rendered output, numbered as RenderedWindow numbers a part of it, for `lint --rendered`.
- `Options` (type): Options configure one render.

- `SourceWindow` (func): SourceWindow is the template source around a template error, numbered and marked, or "" when err is not one or names another file -- an error inside an imported file is that file's, and src is not.

## `internal/rendersandbox`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/rendersandbox`.

Package rendersandbox is SPEC section 25.4's render sandbox: YAML parsing and template rendering in an unprivileged child process.

### Why a child at all

SPEC's argument is one sentence and it is the whole design: "the parser and the template engine are the largest and most attacker-adjacent code in the system, and they need no privilege at all". A state tree is attacker-adjacent because it arrives from a file server, from gitfs, or from whoever can commit to the repository the tree lives in, and the node that renders it runs as root because package and service management require it. Everything between those two facts is this package.

### What crosses the boundary

Data, in both directions, and nothing else. The parent sends the file body, the stage list, and the context a template may read: grains, pillar, the redacted configuration, the environment names. The child sends back the parsed value with its source positions intact, the rendered text, and the warnings.

Two things the child cannot do for itself come back as callbacks. A template that includes another one needs the parent, which is the only side that can reach the hub's file server. And \`salt\['pkg.version']\` needs the parent, because module execution is the privilege being withheld. SPEC 25.4 is explicit that this is the shape: "module execution happens in the privileged parent ... the sandbox returns data, never a callable and never a command to run without validation".

### What it does not protect against

Stated here rather than left to be discovered. A template that calls an execution module still causes the parent to run that module, and a tree that can write \`{{ salt\['cmd.run']('...') }}\` gets the same effect sandboxed or not: that is what the template language is, and the controls for it are RBAC's separate \`arbitrary\_code\` permission and the signed-tree work of SPEC 25.1. What moves into the child is the code that parses and evaluates the attacker's \*text\* -- the lexer, the parser, the evaluator, the YAML reader -- so that a memory-safety or logic defect in any of them lands in a process that owns nothing.

### Honesty about enforcement

\`Describe\` reports what is actually applied on the machine in front of the operator, in the manner of the bridge sandbox of SPEC 24.3. A process boundary holds everywhere. Dropping to an unprivileged account needs a parent that is root and an account to drop to. Denying the network needs a mechanism that only Linux has here. None of it is silently skipped and none of it is claimed where it is not applied.

**Files:** `child.go`, `codec.go`, `confine_linux.go`, `confine_other.go`, `confine_unix.go`, `frame.go`, `lookup_unix.go`, `sandbox.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Config` (type): Config is how a sandbox is set up.
- `New` (func): New returns a sandbox.
- `Sandbox` (type): Sandbox is a render.Engine that renders in a child process.
- `Serve` (func): Serve runs the child protocol until stdin closes.

## `internal/regexcompat`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/regexcompat`.

Package regexcompat is the honest limitation of SPEC section 10.4 made mechanical.

Go's regexp package implements RE2, which guarantees linear-time matching and therefore has no backreferences, no lookahead, no lookbehind, no atomic groups, and no recursion. Python's re, which Salt uses, has all of them.

The rule this package enforces: a pattern using a construct RE2 lacks is a hard error naming the construct, never a silent non-match. A silent non-match in file.replace is a state that reports success and changes nothing, which is the worst available outcome.

**Files:** `regexcompat.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Compile` (func): Compile builds a pattern, reporting an unsupported construct by name rather than letting RE2's own message confuse the reader.
- `CompileWithFlags` (func): CompileWithFlags applies Python's inline flag spellings that RE2 shares, so a pattern carried over from a Salt tree compiles unchanged.
- `Construct` (type): Construct is one unsupported piece of a pattern.
- `Error` (type): Error is a refusal to compile a pattern, naming what RE2 lacks.
- `Unsupported` (func): Unsupported reports every construct in a pattern that RE2 cannot express.

## `internal/state`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/state`.

Package state is halite's state compiler: SLS declarations in, an ordered list of executable low chunks out.

The compiler reproduces Salt's semantics including the parts that are surprising, because a tree that has been in production for years depends on the surprising parts. Where it departs, it departs on purpose and the departure is named in a comment and in SPEC section 11.

One departure is worth stating up front: every error is collected and reported together. Salt reports the first and stops, which makes fixing a large tree an iterative grind. SPEC section 11.2 step 10.

## `internal/states`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/states`.

Package states is the state module surface.

The test-mode contract of SPEC section 11.6 is a first-class part of it, not a suggestion: in test mode a function must make no change, return a nil result when it would change something, populate changes with the predicted change, and populate comment with a human sentence. Conformance is enforced by the shared harness in this package. Salt has no such harness, which is why test=True in Salt is unreliable for a nontrivial fraction of modules.

This used to say the harness is one "which every state module must pass", which was an intention rather than a fact: eighteen of a hundred and thirty-two functions had a case, and nothing said which the rest were. The harness \*applies\* the state, twice, for real -- that is how idempotence becomes observable, and it is also the limit, because a case can only exist for a function whose whole effect lands inside a directory the test owns. \`pkg.installed\` and \`service.running\` would apply to the machine running the suite.

So the obligation is written down instead of asserted: \`internal/builtin\`'s \`unconformed\` table holds every function without a case and why, and a new state function with neither a case nor an entry fails. Thirty-five of the hundred and thirty-two have a case and ninety-seven are listed there, all of them needing either the node's own roots or a machine nobody minds breaking.

Not every state has work to do. \`cmd.wait\` and \`module.wait\` act only when a watch requisite fires, and the \`test.\*\` fakes report a fixed answer, so for them idempotence is free and the contract is that the answer does not depend on the mode -- which is what \`Conformance.Unchanging\` checks. DIVERGENCE 5.157.

**Files:** `conformance.go`, `states.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Bool` (func): Bool reads a boolean argument, with a default.
- `Change` (func): Change builds the {old, new} pair Salt's changes mapping uses.
- `Changed` (func): Changed marks a success that made changes.
- `CommentIsASentence` (func): CommentIsASentence is checkComment, for an audit outside this package.
- `Conformance` (type): Conformance is the shared harness of SPEC section 11.6 that every state module must pass.
- `Failure` (type): Failure is one conformance violation.
- `False` (func): False marks a failure.
- `Func` (type): Func is one state function.
- `Int` (func): Int reads an integer argument, with a default.
- `Mapping` (func): Mapping reads a mapping argument.
- `Module` (type): Module is a state function together with its signature and, where the module supports `watch`, its mod_watch reaction.
- `NewRegistry` (func): NewRegistry returns an empty registry.
- `Registry` (type): Registry holds the state modules a build ships.

## `internal/runner`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/runner`.

Package runner executes a compiled low state.

The compiler decided what runs and in what order. This package decides whether each chunk runs at all — requisite gating, the universal unless/onlyif/creates gates, the prereq two-phase run — and carries the result forward so the next chunk can see it.

## `internal/exec`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/exec`.

Package exec is the execution module surface: the registry, the calling convention, and the context a module function runs in.

A module function receives its arguments already bound and type-checked against its signature, so a function body never has to guess what it was handed. That is what the build-time signatures of SPEC section 15.6 buy.

## `internal/signature`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/signature`.

Package signature is the machine-readable description of every module function: its parameters, their types, whether it changes the system, whether it honours test mode, which platforms it applies to, and what privilege it needs.

Salt derives this by Python introspection at runtime. Here it is declared at build time, which is what lets the state compiler validate a whole tree without executing anything. SPEC section 15.6. SPEC 11.9's \`halite-hub state.compile\`, which would gate a tree in CI this way, is not built (DIVERGENCE 6.4); this comment used to say it was.

**Files:** `platform.go`, `signature.go`, `wire.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `ArgError` (type): ArgError is a rejected argument, naming the parameter and why.
- `FromWire` (func): FromWire converts a received signature, resolving the type names.
- `NamedType` (func): NamedType resolves a wire type name.
- `NewRegistry` (func): NewRegistry returns an empty registry.
- `Param` (type): Param is one parameter of a function.
- `PlatformError` (type): PlatformError is returned when a function cannot run here at all.
- `Registry` (type): Registry holds the signatures a build ships.
- `Signature` (type): Signature describes one `module.function`.
- `TestMode` (type): TestMode states how honestly a function behaves under test=True.
- `Type` (type): Type is a parameter's declared type.

## `internal/target`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/target`.

Package target evaluates a target expression against a node.

Targeting is evaluated on the hub, against the last-known grains, pillar, and connection state of each node. Salt evaluates most target types on the managed endpoint instead, which means every endpoint sees every job, and a compromised one learns the target expression and arguments of jobs meant for others. Here a node receives only the jobs it matched. SPEC section 8.

The same matchers evaluate a top file, which is why this package is shared by the state compiler and the pillar compiler.

**Files:** `compound.go`, `target.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Compile` (func): Compile prepares a target expression of the given kind.
- `CompileAuto` (func): CompileAuto guesses the kind from the expression, which is how a top file entry is written: a bare glob unless it carries a compound sigil.
- `Error` (type): Error is an unparseable or unusable expression.
- `Kind` (type): Kind names a target type.
- `KindFromFlag` (func): KindFromFlag resolves a CLI flag letter to a kind.
- `ListIDs` (func): ListIDs splits a list target, flag -L, into the node IDs it names: comma-separated, each trimmed, empty elements dropped.
- `MatchGlob` (func): MatchGlob reports whether a node ID matches a glob, by the same rule the fleet is targeted with.
- `Matcher` (type): Matcher is a compiled target expression.
- `Node` (type): Node is everything a matcher may read about one node.
- `Nodegroups` (type): Nodegroups resolves a nodegroup name to its expression.
- `Term` (type): Term is one leaf of a compiled target: what it consults, and by what key where it has one.
- `ValidateNodegroups` (func): ValidateNodegroups checks every nodegroup at load rather than at use, so that a cycle or a missing reference is a configuration error the operator sees at start.

## `internal/pillar`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/pillar`.

Package pillar compiles a node's pillar.

Pillar is the secret-bearing path, so two properties matter more here than anywhere else. An external source that fails is a hard error rather than a partial pillar, because a partial pillar silently applies a state with a missing value. And the grains a node may target on are an allowlist, because a node controls its own grains and could otherwise claim \`role: database\` and be handed the database pillar. SPEC sections 12.4 and 12.7.

**Files:** `ext.go`, `pillar.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `AuditEntry` (type): AuditEntry records why one pillar SLS was delivered to this node.
- `Compiled` (type): Compiled is a node's pillar and the record of how it was assembled.
- `Compiler` (type): Compiler assembles a pillar.
- `Config` (type): Config controls a compilation.
- `ExtRequest` (type): ExtRequest is what a source is asked for.
- `ExtSource` (type): ExtSource is one external pillar source.

## `internal/grains`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/grains`.

Package grains collects facts about the node it runs on.

Everything here comes from the operating system directly, through files and stdlib calls, with no third-party code. On Linux that means /proc, /sys, /etc/os-release, and net.Interfaces rather than dmidecode, lscpu, or ip: grain collection has to work on a minimal image where none of those are installed. SPEC section 14.1.

**Files:** `cloud.go`, `fips.go`, `fqdn.go`, `grains.go`, `platform_bsd.go`, `platform_linux.go`, `platform_windows.go`, `provider_unix.go`, `provider_windows.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `CloudOptions` (type): CloudOptions configure the metadata walk.
- `Collect` (func): Collect gathers the grains for this node.
- `FQDN` (func): FQDN is host's fully qualified name, or host itself when it already has a domain, when nothing qualifies it, or when DNS does not answer within FQDNLookupTimeout.
- `Options` (type): Options control collection.
- `QualifiedName` (func): QualifiedName returns a name that carries a domain, or "".
- `ResolveFQDN` (func): ResolveFQDN is FQDN against a given resolver and deadline.
- `Resolver` (type): Resolver is the part of *net.Resolver the lookup needs, so a test can say what the network answers instead of depending on the machine it runs on.
- `UseResolver` (func): UseResolver makes FQDN ask r and returns what puts the previous one back.
- `Warning` (type): Warning is a collection problem that did not stop the rest.

## `internal/migrate`

Import path `github.com/edlitmus/halite/internal/migrate`.

Package migrate audits an existing Salt tree and reports what halite can compile as written, what has to be translated, and what it does not support at all.

It produces a report, not a rewritten tree, because a tool that silently rewrites a production state tree is not trustworthy. SPEC section 28.5.

The report is meant to run in CI against the existing tree from day one of the project, so the compatibility target is measured continuously rather than guessed.

**Files:** `context.go`, `declarations.go`, `migrate.go`, `pyfunc.go`, `report.go`, `skeleton.go`, `undefined.go`; with tests.

**Exports.**

- `Category` (type): Category names a kind of finding, and is what the effort estimate counts.
- `Counts` (type): Counts summarises the findings by category and severity, which is the effort estimate: a migration can be scoped before it is committed to rather than discovered during it.
- `Finding` (type): Finding is one item in the report.
- `GenerateSkeleton` (func): GenerateSkeleton writes a Go bridge for one Python module.
- `KindForDir` (func): KindForDir answers with the extension kind a Salt directory maps to.
- `Options` (type): Options control an audit.
- `PyFunction` (type): PyFunction is one function found in a Salt custom module.
- `PyModule` (type): PyModule is what one Python file declares.
- `PyParam` (type): PyParam is one parameter.
- `ReadPyModule` (func): ReadPyModule extracts what a Salt custom module declares.
- `Report` (type): Report is the whole audit.
- `Run` (func): Run audits a tree.
- `Severity` (type): Severity says whether a finding blocks a migration.
- `Skeleton` (type): Skeleton is a generated Go bridge for one Salt custom module.
- `Skeletons` (func): Skeletons generates a bridge for every custom module in a report, in path order so two runs produce the same set.
